answer.diagnosis: The structured layer-1 units split into two families. Family A (units 3,7,8,21,22,24,27,28) has a positive disk with a negative centre; it detects large blobs and feeds positive-logit units such as L2 u1. Family B (units 2,4,14,17,18,19,25,26,29,30) has a positive centre and a negative annulus; it detects small blobs and feeds the negative-logit units L2 u9 and u11. These size filters are legitimate. Beyond them, both families carry large, sign-consistent weights on specific isolated pixels in the image border and background, outside the blob region. These weights are as large as the strongest blob weights (up to ~99) and well above the init range (~±21). Pixels such as (1,0), (1,16), (1,17), (3,5), (3,12), (8,0), (8,2), (16,21), (19,0), (19,2), (20,19), (21,4), (21,14) and (23,7) are strongly positive in family B and strongly negative in family A, so they vote 'small'. Pixels such as (0,4), (0,11), (0,17), (0,19), (1,4), (1,23), (23,1), (23,4) and (23,11) have the opposite signs and vote 'large'. Blob position and background noise vary from image to image, so the consistent cross-unit reliance on fixed background pixels most likely reflects a fixed pixel pattern (watermark-like) correlated with the label. The weights alone cannot rule out overfitting to a small training set, so confidence is moderate. Fix: in every structured unit, I replace the border/background weights (rows 0-3, rows 20-23, cols 0-3 and cols 20-23, plus the inner 2x2 corners) with a constant. Each constant is my eyeballed estimate of that unit's mean border weight. This removes pixel-specific sensitivity while roughly preserving the bias-like contribution from overall background brightness. The central blob filters, which carry the size computation, are untouched.

answer.diagnosis: The structured layer-1 units split into two families. Family A (units 3,7,8,21,22,24,27,28) has a positive disk with a negative centre; it detects large blobs and feeds positive-logit units such as L2 u1. Family B (units 2,4,14,17,18,19,25,26,29,30) has a positive centre and a negative annulus; it detects small blobs and feeds the negative-logit units L2 u9 and u11. These size filters are legitimate. Beyond them, both families carry large, sign-consistent weights on specific isolated pixels in the image border and background, outside the blob region. These weights are as large as the strongest blob weights (up to ~99) and well above the init range (~±21). Pixels such as (1,0), (1,16), (1,17), (3,5), (3,12), (8,0), (8,2), (16,21), (19,0), (19,2), (20,19), (21,4), (21,14) and (23,7) are strongly positive in family B and strongly negative in family A, so they vote 'small'. Pixels such as (0,4), (0,11), (0,17), (0,19), (1,4), (1,23), (23,1), (23,4) and (23,11) have the opposite signs and vote 'large'. Blob position and background noise vary from image to image, so the consistent cross-unit reliance on fixed background pixels most likely reflects a fixed pixel pattern (watermark-like) correlated with the label. The weights alone cannot rule out overfitting to a small training set, so confidence is moderate. Fix: in every structured unit, I replace the border/background weights (rows 0-3, rows 20-23, cols 0-3 and cols 20-23, plus the inner 2x2 corners) with a constant. Each constant is my eyeballed estimate of that unit's mean border weight. This removes pixel-specific sensitivity while roughly preserving the bias-like contribution from overall background brightness. The central blob filters, which carry the size computation, are untouched.
